title: Therma-Shift coaster
description: A dual mode thermoelectric coaster that heats or cools any mug or glass. Bench validated to 11 C on the cold face at 12 V, with thermal runaway protection.
og_alt: Airflow illustration of the Therma-Shift coaster heat sink.
lede: A solid state desktop coaster that heats or cools any mug, glass or can.
clip_aria: Airflow illustration: air enters all bottom grille slots, passes through the heatsink fins, descends into the blower and exits the oval side vent. Heating and cooling use the same flow direction.

brief.label: Status
brief.value: Thermal stack validated, electronics in progress

brief_note: Heated mugs lock you into their cup. Cheap USB warmers have no temperature control.

stats.label: Cold face at 12 V, steady state
Modes from one stack, by polarity

sections.label: The problem
paras: The coaster has to run unattended on a desk.

sections.label: Constraints
cards: Universal: any mug, glass or can, the device adapts to the drinkware
Dual mode, heating and cooling from the same hardware
Powered over USB-C Power Delivery, within a desk power budget
Thermal runaway prevention independent of the control loop
Low profile and quiet enough for an office desk

sections.label: The design
paras: A thermoelectric module heats or cools depending on current direction. The TEC1-12703 sits between an aluminum top plate and a finned heatsink with a blower.
An NTC thermistor at the plate closes the loop, targeting about 2 degrees F around setpoint.
Separate firmware cutoffs watch for thermal runaway independently of the control loop and shut the device down on a fault.

sections.label: Bench test
paras: Before adding any control loop, I bench tested the bare thermal stack on a lab supply with K-type thermocouples on both faces.

sections.label: Where it stands
list: 10.7 to 12 degrees C cold face at 12 V, steady state
Dual mode verified: the same stack heats and cools by polarity
Staged firmware test suite written; closed loop integration in progress
